notes.definition: Cracking is the breaking down of large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful molecules. It is done by catalytic cracking or steam cracking, and the products include smaller alkanes and alkenes. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and turn orange bromine water colourless.
explanation: Fractional distillation produces more long-chain hydrocarbons than are needed, and not enough of the short-chain ones. There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules, such as petrol, because they flow and ignite easily. Cracking solves this problem: it breaks large hydrocarbon molecules down into smaller, more useful molecules. Cracking is a thermal decomposition reaction, because heat is used to break the large molecules apart.

There are two methods of cracking. In catalytic cracking, the heavy fraction is heated to vaporise it, and the vapour is passed over a hot catalyst (for example a powdered mineral such as aluminium oxide or a zeolite) at a temperature of around 550 °C. In steam cracking, the hydrocarbon vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature (around 800 °C). In the laboratory, liquid paraffin soaked into mineral wool can be heated so that its vapour passes over hot broken pottery, which acts as a catalyst.

The products of cracking include alkanes and another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes. Alkenes contain a carbon to carbon double bond (C=C). For example, decane can be cracked to produce octane (an alkane) and ethene (an alkene): C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. A cracking equation must be balanced: the total numbers of carbon and hydrogen atoms on each side must be equal. Because the long chain can break in different places, the same starting alkane can give different products.

Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes. This is shown by the test for alkenes: when an alkene is shaken with bromine water, the bromine water changes from orange to colourless. Alkanes do not react, so the bromine water stays orange. This difference is evidence that alkenes are more reactive than alkanes, because the double bond can react with bromine.

The products of cracking are very useful. The smaller alkanes are used as fuels, such as petrol, which helps meet the high demand. The alkenes are used to produce polymers (plastics such as poly(ethene)) and as starting materials for making many other chemicals. Modern life depends on hydrocarbons from crude oil: they provide fuels for transport, heating and electricity, and the raw materials for plastics, solvents, detergents and medicines.
keyFacts: Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful molecules.
Cracking is a thermal decomposition reaction.
Catalytic cracking: vaporise the hydrocarbon and pass it over a hot catalyst.
Steam cracking: mix the hydrocarbon vapour with steam and heat to a very high temperature.
The products of cracking are smaller alkanes and alkenes.
Alkenes contain a C=C double bond and are more reactive than alkanes.
Test for alkenes: bromine water turns from orange to colourless.
Small alkanes from cracking are used as fuels because demand is high.
Alkenes are used to make polymers and as starting materials for other chemicals.
Cracking equations must have the same number of C and H atoms on each side.

keyTerms.definition: Breaking down large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful molecules, using heat and a catalyst or steam.
Breaking down a substance into simpler substances using heat.
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a hot catalyst.
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon to carbon double bond (C=C).

workedExamples.title: Finding a missing product
workedExamples.question: Complete the cracking equation: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + ____
steps: Carbon: 12 on the left, 8 on the right, so the missing product has 12 − 8 = 4 C atoms.
Hydrogen: 26 on the left, 18 on the right, so the missing product has 26 − 18 = 8 H atoms.
The missing product is C₄H₈, an alkene (it has twice as many H as C).

workedExamples.title: Balancing a cracking equation
workedExamples.question: Hexadecane is cracked: C₁₆H₃₄ → C₁₀H₂₂ + xC₃H₆. Find the value of x.
steps: Carbon: 16 − 10 = 6 C atoms left for the alkene.
Each C₃H₆ has 3 C atoms, so x = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

workedExamples.title: Evidence that alkenes are more reactive
workedExamples.question: Describe how to show that the gas collected from cracking contains an alkene.
steps: Add a few drops of orange bromine water to the gas in a test tube.
If an alkene is present the bromine water turns from orange to colourless. An alkane would leave it orange.
workedExamples.answer: Bromine water decolourises (orange to colourless), showing an alkene is present.

diagrams.title: A cracking equation
diagrams.caption: Hexane can be cracked into butane (a smaller alkane) and ethene (an alkene with a C=C double bond): C₆H₁₄ → C₄H₁₀ + C₂H₄. There are 6 C and 14 H atoms on each side.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cracking only produces alkenes.
misconceptions.right: In fact cracking produces a mixture of smaller alkanes and alkenes (and sometimes hydrogen).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say bromine water goes 'clear' with an alkene.
misconceptions.right: In fact it turns colourless. 'Clear' means see-through, and orange bromine water is already clear.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse cracking with fractional distillation.
misconceptions.right: In fact fractional distillation separates molecules by boiling point (physical), while cracking breaks covalent bonds to make new, smaller molecules (chemical).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cracking is done to get rid of large molecules that are useless.
misconceptions.right: In fact cracking matches supply to demand: it turns less useful large molecules into high-demand fuels and alkenes for making polymers.

realWorld: Oil refineries use catalytic crackers to turn heavy fractions into extra petrol, because supply from distillation alone is less than demand.
Ethene from steam cracking is the starting material for poly(ethene), used in carrier bags and bottles.
Propene from cracking is used to make poly(propene) for ropes, crates and food containers.
separateOnlyContent: Alkenes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ (covered fully in Structure and formulae of alkenes).
Alkenes react by addition across the C=C double bond; the bromine water test is an addition reaction that forms a colourless dibromo compound.
examTips: Describe conditions in general terms: catalytic cracking uses heat and a catalyst; steam cracking uses steam and a very high temperature.
For cracking equations, subtract carbons and hydrogens separately to find a missing product, then check both totals.
Always give both colours for the bromine water test: orange to colourless.
Explain why we crack: supply of large molecules exceeds demand, while demand for small molecules (fuels) exceeds supply, and alkenes are needed for polymers.
summary: Cracking breaks large hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules.
Catalytic cracking uses a hot catalyst; steam cracking uses steam and a very high temperature.
Products include smaller alkanes and alkenes.
Alkenes have a C=C double bond and are more reactive than alkanes.
Bromine water turns from orange to colourless with alkenes.
Small alkanes are used as fuels; alkenes are used to make polymers and other chemicals.

questions.question: Which of these describes cracking?
options: Joining small molecules into large ones
Breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones
markScheme: 1 mark: breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks bonds in large molecules to form smaller, more useful molecules. Separating into fractions is fractional distillation.

questions.question:
An alkene is shaken with bromine water.
What is the colour change?
markScheme: 1 mark: orange to colourless
questions.explanation: Bromine water is orange. It reacts with the C=C bond of the alkene and becomes colourless.

questions.question:
Cracking produces alkanes and one other type of hydrocarbon.
Which type of hydrocarbon is also produced by cracking?
markScheme: 1 mark: alkenes
questions.explanation: Cracking produces smaller alkanes and alkenes. Alcohols and acids contain oxygen so are not hydrocarbons.

options: Hydrocarbon vapour passed over a hot catalyst
Cooling the hydrocarbon in a fractionating column
markScheme: 1 mark: vapour passed over a hot catalyst
questions.explanation: The hydrocarbon is vaporised and passed over a hot catalyst. Steam cracking uses steam and a very high temperature, not a low one.

questions.question: Why do oil companies carry out cracking?
options: To remove impurities such as sulfur
To separate crude oil into fractions
To produce more small molecules, which are in high demand
To make long-chain hydrocarbons for fuel oil
markScheme: 1 mark: to make more small molecules which are in high demand
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation produces too many large molecules and not enough small ones like petrol, so large molecules are cracked.

questions.question:
Tetradecane is cracked.
C₁₄H₃₀ → C₁₀H₂₂ + ____
Which is the missing product?
markScheme: 1 mark: C₄H₈
questions.explanation: C: 14 − 10 = 4. H: 30 − 22 = 8. The product is C₄H₈ (butene).

questions.question: Which observation shows that alkenes are more reactive than alkanes?
options: Alkenes burn but alkanes do not
Alkenes dissolve in water but alkanes do not
Alkenes decolourise bromine water but alkanes do not
markScheme: 1 mark: alkenes decolourise bromine water but alkanes do not
questions.explanation: Under the same conditions bromine reacts with alkenes but not alkanes. Both alkanes and alkenes burn.

questions.question: Which is a main use of the alkenes produced by cracking?
markScheme: 1 mark: making polymers
questions.explanation: Alkenes such as ethene and propene are used to make polymers and as starting materials for many other chemicals.

questions.question:
Octane can be cracked.
C₈H₁₈ → C₄H₁₀ + 2X
What is the formula of X?
markScheme: 1 mark: C₂H₄
questions.explanation: C: 8 − 4 = 4, H: 18 − 10 = 8 shared between 2 molecules, so each X is C₂H₄. C₄H₈ would be correct only for 1X.

questions.question:
Decane is cracked to produce hexane and an alkene.
C₁₀H₂₂ → C₆H₁₄ + CₐH₈
Calculate the value of a, the number of carbon atoms in one molecule of the alkene.
markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: Carbon must balance: 10 − 6 = 4. The alkene is C₄H₈ (hydrogen check: 14 + 8 = 22).

questions.question:
An alkane is cracked.
C₁₈H₃₈ → C₁₂H₂₆ + xC₂H₄
Calculate the value of x.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon left = 18 − 12 = 6
questions.explanation: Check hydrogen: 26 + 3 × 4 = 38. Both C and H balance when x = 3.

questions.question:
Pentadecane is cracked.
C₁₅H₃₂ → C₉H₂₀ + C₆Hₓ
Calculate the value of x, the number of hydrogen atoms in one molecule of the second product.
markScheme: 1 mark: 12
questions.explanation: Hydrogen must balance: 32 − 20 = 12, giving C₆H₁₂.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the displayed formula of ethene, C₂H₄.
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of ethene.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12   H = 1
markScheme: 1 mark: 28
questions.explanation: Two carbon atoms give 2 × 12 = 24 and four hydrogen atoms give 4 × 1 = 4, so Mr = 28.

questions.question:
Dodecane, C₁₂H₂₆, is cracked to form one molecule of hexane, C₆H₁₄, and some molecules of propene, C₃H₆.
Calculate the number of propene molecules formed from one molecule of dodecane.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon remaining 12 − 6 = 6
1 mark: hydrogen remaining 26 − 14 = 12
1 mark: 2 propene molecules (6 C and 12 H = 2 × C₃H₆)
questions.explanation: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₆H₁₄ + 2C₃H₆. Checking both elements confirms the answer.

questions.question:
A refinery cracks 500 tonnes of a heavy fraction.
All of the fraction is converted into products.
Table 1 shows the percentage by mass of each type of product.
Calculate the mass of alkenes produced.
markScheme: 1 mark: mass of products = 500 tonnes (mass conserved)
1 mark: 0.38 × 500 = 190 tonnes
questions.explanation: Mass is conserved in cracking, so the products have a total mass of 500 tonnes; 38% of 500 = 190 tonnes.

questions.question: Name the reagent used to test for alkenes.
markScheme: 1 mark: bromine water
questions.explanation: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless when shaken with an alkene.

questions.question: Give two uses of the products of cracking.
markScheme: 1 mark: smaller alkanes used as fuels
1 mark: alkenes used to make polymers / other chemicals
questions.explanation: The small alkanes meet the demand for fuels; alkenes are used for polymers and as chemical feedstock.

questions.question: Describe the conditions used in steam cracking.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrocarbon (vapour) mixed with steam
1 mark: heated to a very high temperature
questions.explanation: Steam cracking does not use a catalyst; it relies on steam and a very high temperature.

questions.question:
A student shakes two gases, A and B, with bromine water.
Table 1 shows the results.
Identify which gas is an alkene.
Explain what the results show.

headers: Colour of bromine water after shaking

markScheme: 1 mark: gas A is the alkene
1 mark: alkenes are more reactive than alkanes / B is (probably) an alkane that does not react
questions.explanation: Only the alkene reacts with bromine, removing the orange colour.

questions.question: Explain why cracking is described as a thermal decomposition reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: heat is used (thermal)
1 mark: a large molecule is broken down into smaller molecules (decomposition)
questions.explanation: Thermal means using heat; decomposition means breaking down into simpler substances.

questions.question: Explain how modern life depends on the uses of hydrocarbons from crude oil, including the products of cracking.
markScheme: 1 mark: fuels for transport (petrol, diesel, kerosene)
1 mark: fuels for heating / generating electricity
1 mark: alkenes from cracking make polymers / plastics and other chemicals (e.g. solvents, detergents)
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons supply most transport fuels and the starting materials for plastics and many chemicals.

markScheme: Indicative content: soak mineral wool in liquid paraffin at the end of a boiling tube; place broken pottery / aluminium oxide catalyst in the middle; heat the catalyst strongly, then warm the paraffin so vapour passes over the hot catalyst; collect gas over water in a test tube; remove delivery tube from water before stopping heating; add bromine water to the gas and shake; orange to colourless shows an alkene.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear method including heating catalyst and collecting gas, plus correct bromine water test with colour change.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple method or test only.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both the cracking method and the test with the full colour change.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the supply from fractional distillation and the demand for two fractions.
Use the data in Table 1 to explain why oil refineries crack hydrocarbons.
In your answer, include:
• the types of products and their uses
• the conditions for cracking
• an example of a balanced cracking equation.
markScheme: Indicative content: demand for petrol exceeds supply (30% vs 20%); supply of heavy fuel oil exceeds demand (25% vs 10%); cracking converts surplus large molecules into smaller, more useful ones; products are smaller alkanes, used as fuels like petrol, and alkenes, used to make polymers and other chemicals; catalytic cracking: vaporise and pass over hot catalyst; steam cracking: mix with steam, very high temperature; example equation e.g. C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ with C and H balanced; small molecules are in demand because they flow and ignite easily.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): uses data to compare supply and demand for both fractions, describes both cracking methods, gives products and uses, and a correctly balanced equation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): refers to data and explains cracking with some conditions or products; equation may contain errors.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. cracking makes small molecules, with little use of data.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key idea is matching supply to demand. A strong answer quotes the numbers, gives conditions for both methods and a balanced equation.

questions.question: Which statement about cracking is correct?
options: It is a physical process that separates molecules by boiling point
It breaks covalent bonds to produce new, smaller molecules
It always produces only one product
markScheme: 1 mark: it breaks covalent bonds to produce new smaller molecules
questions.explanation: Cracking is a chemical reaction (thermal decomposition). Separation by boiling point is fractional distillation, and cracking gives a mixture of products, including alkenes.

questions.question: Give the purpose of the catalyst in catalytic cracking.
markScheme: 1 mark: speeds up the reaction (without being used up)
questions.explanation: The hot catalyst speeds up the breaking of the large molecules and is not used up.
